title: Introduction to Microeconomics
description: Class 11 Economics: microeconomics vs macroeconomics, positive vs normative economics, the central problems of an economy, scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and the production possibility curve.

topics.title: Microeconomics, Macroeconomics and Positive vs Normative
topics.concept:
Economics studies how a society uses its scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. The subject is divided into two broad branches depending on what is being studied:

  • Microeconomics — studies the economic behaviour of individual units: a single consumer, a single firm, a single market, the price of one good. The word "micro" means small. It deals with topics like demand, supply, price of a product, and consumer and producer behaviour. (It is sometimes called price theory.)
  • Macroeconomics — studies the economy as a whole: total (aggregate) output, national income, total employment, the general price level and inflation. The word "macro" means large. (It is sometimes called income theory.) This Class-11 course focuses mainly on microeconomics.

Economics can also be divided by the type of statement it makes:

  • Positive economics — deals with facts and "what is"; its statements can be tested as true or false (e.g. "a rise in price reduces demand").
  • Normative economics — deals with opinions and "what ought to be"; it involves value judgements that cannot simply be proved true or false (e.g. "the government should give free education").

So microeconomics looks at the small parts, macroeconomics at the whole; positive economics describes, while normative economics prescribes.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics?
examples.solution:
It depends on the level studied.

  • Microeconomics studies individual units (a consumer, a firm, one market/price).
  • Macroeconomics studies the whole economy (national income, total employment, general price level).
examples.answer: Microeconomics studies individual units (a consumer, firm or market); macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole.

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify: (a) 'A rise in price reduces demand', (b) 'The poor should pay no tax'.
examples.solution:
Fact vs opinion.

  • (a) is a testable fact — positive economics.
  • (b) is a value judgement (what ought to be) — normative economics.
examples.answer: (a) Positive economics (a fact); (b) Normative economics (a value judgement).

examples.problem: Example 3: Studying the total national income of a country belongs to which branch?
examples.solution:
National income is an aggregate.

  • It studies the economy as a whole.
  • So it is macroeconomics.

recap:
• Microeconomics = individual units (consumer, firm, one market/price; 'price theory'). Macroeconomics = whole economy (national income, employment, price level; 'income theory').
  • Positive economics = 'what is' (testable facts); Normative = 'what ought to be' (value judgements).

quiz.q: The study of a single firm or a single market is part of:
quiz.explanation: Individual units are studied in microeconomics.

quiz.q: 'The government ought to provide free healthcare' is a ____ statement.
quiz.explanation: It is a value judgement (what ought to be) — normative economics.

topics.title: Scarcity, Choice and the Central Problems of an Economy
topics.concept:
The whole of economics springs from one basic fact: scarcity. Human wants are unlimited, but the resources (land, labour, capital) to satisfy them are limited, and those resources have alternative uses. Because we cannot have everything, we must choose — and every choice means giving something up. So economics is often called the science of choice.

The cost of a choice is measured by its opportunity cost — the value of the next-best alternative that is given up. For example, if a farmer uses his land to grow wheat, the opportunity cost is the rice he could have grown instead. Opportunity cost is one of the most important ideas in economics: the "real" cost of anything is what you sacrifice to get it.

Because of scarcity, every economy — rich or poor — must answer three central problems (the basic economic problems of allocation):

  • What to produce — which goods and services, and in what quantities (e.g. more food or more weapons)?
  • How to produce — by which method/technique (labour-intensive or machine-intensive)?
  • For whom to produce — how should the output be distributed among people (who gets how much)?

These problems exist because resources are scarce relative to wants. Solving them well means using resources efficiently so that society gets the most satisfaction from its limited means.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why does the economic problem of choice arise?
examples.solution:
It comes from scarcity.

  • Wants are unlimited but resources are limited and have alternative uses.
  • So we cannot satisfy all wants and must choose.
examples.answer: Because wants are unlimited but resources are scarce and have alternative uses, forcing us to choose.

examples.problem: Example 2: A student spends an evening studying instead of watching a film. What is the opportunity cost?
examples.solution:
It is the next-best alternative given up.

  • The next-best use of that time was watching the film.
examples.answer: The film (the enjoyment of watching it) that was given up — the next-best alternative.

examples.problem: Example 3: State the three central problems of an economy.
examples.solution:
They concern allocation.

  • What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.
examples.answer: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.

recap:
• Scarcity: unlimited wants vs limited resources (with alternative uses) → forces choice.
  • Opportunity cost = value of the next-best alternative given up.
  • Three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce.
  • Goal: use scarce resources efficiently.

quiz.q: The root cause of all economic problems is:
quiz.explanation: Scarcity (unlimited wants vs limited resources) is the root cause.

quiz.q: Opportunity cost is the value of the:
quiz.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative foregone.

topics.title: The Production Possibility Curve (PPC)
topics.concept:
The ideas of scarcity, choice and opportunity cost can be shown in one neat diagram: the Production Possibility Curve (PPC), also called the production possibility frontier. It shows the different combinations of two goods that an economy can produce using all its resources fully and efficiently, with a given technology.

Suppose an economy produces only two goods — say guns and butter. If it puts all resources into butter it makes a lot of butter and no guns; if all into guns, the reverse. In between, it can produce various combinations. Joining these combinations gives the PPC, shown below:

examples.problem: Example 1: What does the production possibility curve show?
examples.solution:
It maps the choices open to an economy.

  • The different combinations of two goods an economy can produce.
  • Using all its resources fully and efficiently with given technology.
examples.answer: The PPC shows the different combinations of two goods an economy can produce by using all its resources fully and efficiently.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why does the PPC slope downward?
examples.solution:
Resources are fixed.

  • To produce more of one good, resources must be shifted away from the other.
  • So more of one means less of the other — a downward slope (opportunity cost).
examples.answer: Because resources are limited, producing more of one good means producing less of the other — reflecting opportunity cost.

examples.problem: Example 3: What does a point lying inside the PPC (point U) indicate?
examples.solution:
It is below the frontier.

  • Resources are not being fully or efficiently used (under-utilisation / unemployment).
examples.answer: Under-utilisation of resources (inefficiency or unemployment) — the economy could produce more.

recap:
• PPC shows combinations of two goods producible with full, efficient use of resources.
  • It slopes downward (more of one = less of the other → opportunity cost) and is concave to the origin (rising opportunity cost).
  • Point on PPC = efficient; inside = under-utilisation; outside = unattainable (with current resources).
  • The PPC shifts right with economic growth.

quiz.q: A point lying outside (beyond) the PPC is:
quiz.explanation: Points beyond the PPC cannot be reached with current resources and technology.

quiz.q: The PPC slopes downward because of:
options: Opportunity cost (more of one means less of the other)
quiz.explanation: Limited resources mean producing more of one good sacrifices the other.

questions.q: The branch of economics that studies individual units (a firm, a market) is:
questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies individual units.

questions.q: The study of national income and total employment belongs to:
questions.explanation: Economy-wide aggregates are studied in macroeconomics.

questions.q: Microeconomics is also called:
questions.explanation: Microeconomics is also known as price theory.

questions.q: A statement of 'what is' that can be tested as true or false is:
questions.explanation: Positive economics deals with testable facts.

questions.q: 'The rich should be taxed more' is a ____ statement.
questions.explanation: It is a value judgement — normative economics.

questions.q: The root of all economic problems is:
questions.explanation: Scarcity (unlimited wants, limited resources) is the root cause.

questions.q: Economics is often called the science of:
questions.explanation: Because scarcity forces choices, economics is the science of choice.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is the value of the:
questions.explanation: It is the next-best alternative given up.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three central problems of an economy?
questions.explanation: The three problems are what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.q: 'How to produce' refers to the choice of:
questions.explanation: 'How to produce' is about the technique (labour vs machine intensive).

questions.q: The PPC shows combinations of two goods produced using resources:
questions.explanation: The PPC assumes full and efficient use of resources.

questions.q: The PPC slopes downward because:
options: More of one good means less of the other
questions.explanation: Limited resources create a trade-off (opportunity cost).

questions.q: A point inside the PPC shows:
questions.explanation: Inside the PPC means resources are not fully/efficiently used.

questions.q: A point outside the PPC is:
questions.explanation: Beyond the PPC is unattainable with current resources/technology.

questions.q: Economic growth shifts the PPC:
questions.explanation: Growth (more/better resources) shifts the PPC outward to the right.

questions.q: Deciding the price of a single product, like a cup of tea, is a matter for:
questions.explanation: The price of one product is an individual-unit issue — microeconomics.

questions.q: A farmer uses his only field to grow wheat instead of rice. The opportunity cost of the wheat is:
options: The rice he could have grown
The money he spent on seeds
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative foregone — the rice crop given up.

questions.q: If an economy moves from a point inside the PPC to a point on the PPC, it has:
options: Used its idle resources, raising output
questions.explanation: Moving to the frontier means previously idle resources are now fully employed, increasing output.

questions.q: The PPC is concave to the origin because, as more of one good is produced, the opportunity cost:
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit costs more of the other — increasing opportunity cost gives the concave shape.

questions.q: Which pair of statements is positive then normative?
options: 'Unemployment rose to 8%' ; 'The government should create more jobs'
questions.explanation: The first reports a measurable fact (positive); the second gives a value judgement (normative).

questions.q: A new invention that makes all factories more productive will shift the PPC:
questions.explanation: Better technology expands what the economy can produce, shifting the PPC outward.

questions.q: The problem 'for whom to produce' is essentially about the:
questions.explanation: 'For whom' concerns how the produced goods are shared among members of society.

questions.q: During a recession with many unemployed workers, the economy is most likely producing at a point:
questions.explanation: Unemployment means resources are idle, so output lies inside (below) the frontier.

questions.q: Choosing a labour-intensive method over a machine-intensive one answers which central problem?
questions.explanation: The method/technique of production answers 'how to produce'.

questions.q: If wants could somehow be fully satisfied with available resources, the basic economic problem would:
options: Disappear, since there would be no scarcity
questions.explanation: No scarcity would mean no need to choose — the economic problem itself would vanish.
